abstract: Psychrophilic organisms display a series of physiological adaptations which enable them to thrive in cold environments, yet the dynamics of these processes in living cells remain largely unexplored. Here, we establish super-resolution microscopy and single-molecule tracking (SMT) in the cold-adapted bacterium Psychrobacter cryohalolentis, enabling the investigation of protein dynamics in vivo at high spatiotemporal resolution. For controlled expression of HaloTag fusions in this organism, we developed an inducible plasmid expression system based on a galactose-inducible promoter. As a proof of concept, we followed the AAA+ unfoldase ClpX during steady-state growth and heat shock. At 22 {degrees}C, ClpX diffused as a single population with a media apparent diffusion coefficient of 0.25 m2/s, suggesting that most molecules reside in large complexes. A shift to 32 {degrees}C, above the growth maximum of this strain, broadened the mobility distribution, increasing both slow and fast populations, and transiently redistributed ClpX towards the cell periphery. During recovery the fast population returned to baseline within 5 min, whereas the slow population remained elevated for at least 30 min, suggesting that the two populations reflect distinct processes. SMT in a psychrophilic bacterium thus opens new possibilities to study how cold-adapted microorganisms respond to environmental change at the molecular level.
